questions.title: What constitutes a “pending or reasonably anticipated” enforcement proceeding under FOIA Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: In Farahi v. FBI the D.C. Circuit applied Exemption 7(A) and said that disclosure could interfere with "pending or reasonably anticipated" enforcement proceedings (citing Citizens for Resp & Ethics v DOJ). I'm unclear what actually satisfies this requirement. Does an ongoing investigation that has not yet resulted in criminal charges count as "pending"? How far into the future can a "reasonably anticipated" proceeding stretch? Does several years passing between the agency's original declaration and its updated declaration affect whether those proceedings are still considered pending?

questions.title: How much judicial deference is owed to an FBI’s finding that records were "compiled for law‑enforcement purposes"?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that because the FBI is a law‑enforcement agency its determination that records were compiled for law‑enforcement purposes is entitled to a "fair measure of deference" (citing Campbell v DOJ). I'm trying to understand how strong this presumption is. Is it merely rebuttable unless the requester shows contrary evidence, or must the agency provide detailed factual support linking each document back to specific investigative duties? Are there limits on this deference when national‑security claims are involved?

questions.title: When can an agency satisfy its §552(a)(8)(A)(ii) “segregation” obligation if non‑exempt material is interspersed throughout exempt documents?
questions.question_body: The district court said no reasonable segregation was possible because any non‑exempt material was "interspersed line‑by‑line" throughout the files (citing Mead). I'm confused about how courts decide what counts as reasonable segregation. Does any redaction qualify? Must agencies produce separate files or heavily edited versions? At what point does intermingled text become excusably inseparable such that no portion must be released?

questions.title: Are sealed ex parte declarations valid evidence in FOIA cases, and what procedural safeguards exist for requesters?
questions.question_body: In Farahi, the court relied heavily on an ex parte declaration submitted under seal by Bender, which Farahi did not oppose. The opinion says nothing required putting that analysis on the public record because Farahi did not object. Can a plaintiff challenge an agency’s reliance on material he cannot see? What standards do courts apply when weighing undisclosed affidavits against a requester's right to know?

questions.title: What standards govern an agency’s use of category‑based withholding under FOIA, and how can a requester show those categories are overly broad?
questions.question_body: Farahi complained that the FBI’s "categories" used in its withholding decision were overbroad, but the panel held he forfeited those arguments because he gave no specific explanation why they were insufficiently distinct (citing CREW and Gallant v NLRB). What exactly must an agency demonstrate when it withholds records on a category‑by‑category basis? How specific must those categories be for a court to evaluate whether each exemption applies correctly? What kinds of arguments have succeeded in proving a category is too vague?

questions.title: Why are summary‑judgment rulings in FOIA cases reviewed de novo on appeal?
questions.question_body: The D.C. Circuit says summary judgment decisions involving FOIA exemptions are reviewed de novo (citing Rep Comm for Freedom of the Press v FBI). In most civil cases I thought appellate courts give weight to factual findings made at trial unless clearly erroneous. Why do exemption analyses receive fresh examination at every level? Does this mean the government bears its burden anew on appeal, and how does this affect strategic considerations for both parties?
